title: Reading a Justice by the Numbers
hook: Label a judge 'conservative' and you've explained almost nothing. Code 311 of Barrett's decisions and a sharper pattern appears: she asks whether a ruling reaches further than the authority behind it.
key_points: Feldman codes 311 Supreme Court decisions to characterize Justice Barrett's method rather than her ideological label.
His core finding: she measures the reach of a proposed decision against the strength of the authority offered to support it.
He identifies five recurring components in her reasoning: source of legal authority, governing test, limiting principles, adequacy of the record, and proper disposition.
Her voting overlaps are issue-dependent: 83.6% agreement with Kavanaugh in non-unanimous cases, 91.7% with Gorsuch on First Amendment questions.
Economic and regulatory disputes are where her coalitions are least stable — 70.6% agreement with Kavanaugh, and 9 of her 23 votes joining the liberal justices over three conservative dissents.
The transferable lesson: judicial behavior is measurable, and method often predicts votes better than ideology does.
content_html: Calling a justice "conservative" or "liberal" predicts a lot of votes and explains none of them. Coding hundreds of decisions gets you something better: the question a judge actually asks before signing an opinion.
extra_html: Writing for SCOTUSblog, Adam Feldman analyzes 311 of Justice Amy Coney Barrett's Supreme Court decisions and argues her jurisprudence has a consistent organizing move: she weighs how far a proposed holding reaches against how strong the authority offered for it is. Feldman finds five components recurring in her reasoning — the source of legal authority, the governing test, the limiting principles, whether the record is adequate, and the appropriate disposition. That method, rather than ideology, explains why her alignments shift by subject. She agrees with Justice Kavanaugh in 83.6% of non-unanimous decisions and with Justice Gorsuch in 91.7% of non-unanimous First Amendment cases, but her coalitions loosen in economic and regulatory disputes, where agreement with Kavanaugh falls to 70.6% and where nine of her twenty-three votes joining the liberal justices over three conservative dissents occurred. (This card describes the U.S. Supreme Court; the broader point — that judicial behavior can be measured, and that reasoning method often predicts outcomes better than a left/right label — travels to any high court that publishes signed opinions.)

related.title: Beyond the Swing Justice
related.hook: The 'swing vote' is a lazy model of a nine-member court. Sort four terms of close cases and you get two distinct jobs: building narrow majorities, and bridging the dissents nobody won.

related.title: Nine Justices, Nine Styles
related.hook: One scholar coded 5,095 questions from a full Supreme Court term and found each justice interrogates lawyers in a signature way — a fingerprint of how they think about the law.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: Not All Dissents Are Created Equal
related.hook: Dissent tallies treat a one-line 'I would deny' the same as a fully reasoned opinion. One scholar sorted 386 of them on the emergency docket — and found about half were just bare votes.

flashcards.prompt: What does Feldman identify as the organizing question behind Justice Barrett's opinions?
flashcards.back_html: Whether a ruling's scope matches the authority supporting it — she measures how far a proposed decision reaches against how strong the textual, historical, and precedential grounding for it actually is.

flashcards.prompt: In which area does the analysis find Barrett's voting coalitions least stable?
flashcards.explanation_html: Her agreement with Kavanaugh drops to 70.6% in non-unanimous economic and regulatory cases, versus 83.6% overall — and most of her cross-bloc votes land there.

flashcards.prompt: Why does an empirical profile like this teach more than an ideological label?

choices.text: It shows the reasoning method that drives votes, and where that method cuts against the expected bloc
It proves justices decide cases at random rather than by ideology
It predicts the outcome of every future case with certainty

flashcards.explanation_html: The five-component method explains her issue-dependent alignments — including the cases where she joins the liberal justices — which a single left/right label cannot.
